facts.fact: Name for the term: "cá bột"
Name for the term: "Fry"
Name for the term: "cá hề bột" (used for clownfish fry)
Newly hatched fish have a yolk sac and cannot yet swim freely to find food.
Hatched larvae live off the yolk sac until it is fully absorbed and only then start looking for food. Fry may take up to a few weeks to develop.
Fry have tiny mouths and tiny stomachs, so they need several small meals a day.
Goldfish fry do not eat for their first 40-48 hours. Other species need food right away.
Egg-layers such as killifish, rainbowfish and tetras produce fry too small to eat baby brine shrimp at first.
Feed fry small meals 3-5 times a day.
Very small fry, such as rainbowfish and tetra fry, can be fed green water, infusoria, fry powder (Hikari First Bites) and vinegar eels.
Larger fry, such as livebearer and African cichlid fry, can take crushed flakes, Repashy gel food, and Easy Fry and Small Fish Food.
Live baby brine shrimp (Artemia) are the best overall fry food.
Baby brine shrimp are roughly 400–500 microns. Switch tiny fry to them after a couple of weeks, once they are big enough.
Infusoria are about 20–300 microns and vinegar eels about 50 microns wide and 1–2 mm long.
Angelfish newborns cannot eat powdered flake and need infusoria or baby brine shrimp for the first few days.
Powdered flake is common but not the best fry food. If it is all you have, grind 1-2 tablespoons very fine and feed it from a wet toothpick touched just above the fry.
To portion powdered fry food, dip a small paintbrush in the powder and tap it lightly over the tank.
Powdered fry food floats, so swirl the water when feeding fry that live near the bottom.
Baby brine shrimp are hatched in salt water with aeration at 74–82°F (23–28°C) and are ready in about 18–36 hours.
To hatch Artemia for cá bột, use about 1 g of eggs per 1 L of seawater, or 30 g of non-iodized salt in 1 L of fresh water.
Petmart's method: dissolve 2 teaspoons of coarse salt in 2 L of dechlorinated tap water, aerate for about 1 hour, then add 1/4 teaspoon of Artemia eggs.
Keep the hatching container lit for the first 24 hours. Artemia nauplii appear after roughly 16–20 hours.
Use strong aeration at first, then turn it down once the Artemia eggs have absorbed water, so the eggs are not blown out.

To harvest, turn off the air and let the contents settle. Shells float and nauplii sink. Shine a flashlight at the bottom to gather the nauplii, then siphon them out with a tube about 3 mm in diameter.
Infusoria can be grown in old tank water and mulm with banana peel, catappa leaves or yeast at 78–80°F (26–27°C). A culture lasts 2–4 weeks, so start a new one every 1–2 weeks for a steady supply.
Grow green water (microalgae) in old tank water with fertilizer or fish food under continuous light.
Move fry away from adults with a net breeder or breeder box that has moss for cover, or remove a livebearer mother after she gives birth. Move fry to a larger grow-out tank once they are bigger.
Do daily water changes, or several a week, at first, because heavily fed fry produce a lot of waste.
Frequent small water changes help keep conditions stable for fry.
Use gentle filtration such as a sponge filter and clean it regularly. Cover a hang-on-back filter's intake with a pre-filter sponge so fry are not sucked in.
Flow must be kept low in a fry tank, so its filtration is less efficient. Keep water chemistry stable and the temperature warm.
Sort fry by size, because faster-growing fry can eat or outcompete smaller ones.
In species that do not guard their fry, remove the parents after spawning. Brood-caring species can stay with their fry.
Overfeeding fouls the water and can kill fry. Frequent feeding in a small volume of water degrades it quickly.
High fry losses often come from poor water quality, predation, or not feeding the right foods often enough.
Fry are easily siphoned up during water changes or lost to filter intakes.
Leaving unfertilized eggs that grow fungus can ruin a clutch. Remove them promptly.
Do not use iodized salt to hatch Artemia for cá bột.
"cá hề bột" should get Artemia nauplii under 30 hours old, because older ones are too big for them to eat.
Feeding bobo from unsanitary sources can cause intestinal infection or blockage.
Artemia survives only a few hours in fresh water.
Vietnamese shops sell Artemia as a food for cá bột of fish such as cá La Hán, cá dĩa, cá chép, cá bảy màu and cá Lia Thia (Betta). The pages give no scientific names.
Khai Nhật says the quality of the Artemia on the Vietnamese market is inconsistent, so buying low-quality product is a risk.
